warmup.q: For a year, the program behind the owners' daily takings has put each payment on the day the program handled it. That was almost always the day it happened, a second earlier. Now the team reads the last 30 days of payments again, from the start of the log, to fill a new table. If they ran the old code on that replay, what would the takings show?
options: The same daily totals the owners had been seeing all month
All 30 days of takings on the day the replay ran, and nothing on the days before
Totals that differ a little, only on days when some card readers sent their payments late
An error, because a month-old payment has no record of when it was handled
warmup.why: During a replay, the program handles every payment today, so the old code puts the whole month on today's date and leaves every earlier day at zero. The third option is what the live program really got wrong, and it's tempting because it's true there. Live, a payment is handled within a second of happening, so only late uploads (payments a card reader sent after being offline) landed on the wrong day. A replay breaks that coincidence for every payment at once. The last option fails because the moment of handling is never stored: it's whatever the clock says when the program runs. The fourth section runs this replay.

sections.h: One payment, written once and copied into five stores
sections.html:
Let's follow one card payment. The payments app writes it once, as a row in PostgreSQL, a free database program that many companies run. A database keeps records in tables, much like the sheets of a spreadsheet. (The labs call the shops merchants.)

Within a second, the same payment exists in four more places, each added for a request the others answered badly.

  1. Support staff find a payment by the last four digits of a card, or by a misspelt name. OpenSearch, a search engine (a program built to find text fast), does that.
  2. Two thousand owners refresh their balance all day. Redis, a program that keeps data in memory for very fast reads, holds each shop's balance.
  3. The fraud check needs each card's spending over the last hour, thousands of times a second. A separate store keeps those numbers, the fraud features.
  4. Finance reads two years of payments at once, which would slow down the till if it ran on PostgreSQL. So each night the payments are copied into Iceberg, a format for big tables kept as files on cheap storage.

What a data system is, the course's first lesson, split data into two kinds. The system of record holds the official version of each fact. A new fact is written there first, and when anything disagrees with it, it wins. Derived data is everything worked out from it, and can be thrown away and worked out again. Here PostgreSQL is the system of record, and the other four stores are derived. The café's old notebook had the same split: the notebook of sales was the record, and the total on a sticky note by the till was derived.

Five copies need a rule for staying in step. The tempting one is for the program to write every store itself. That's a dual write, and Two systems, one truth, in the Stream processing track, showed how it fails. Two updates to one payment can reach two stores in opposite orders, and a crash between two writes leaves one store without the change. The stores disagree, and nothing ever notices.

The fix is to write once and copy from a log, a list of changes that only grows at the end, like the notebook. Change data capture (CDC) is a program that reads every change PostgreSQL saves and adds it to the log. Here the log is a topic in Kafka, a program that keeps named logs of messages. Each derived store has its own reader, a consumer, that applies the changes in log order. If the log is the only way into OpenSearch, OpenSearch can only be behind PostgreSQL, or wrong because of a bug, never on a path of its own.

You may be thinking, "Why not write all five at once, all or nothing?" Atomic commit across machines, in the Transactions track, built that with two-phase commit. Its version between different products is XA, and few of these products support it. Worse, an all-or-nothing write stops whenever any one store stops. In the Try it, with the search engine down for three minutes, the all-or-nothing design turns away 9,000 of 30,000 payments. With the log, every payment goes through. The search engine falls 9,000 records behind and catches up 5 seconds after it comes back.

Copying later keeps a fault inside the store that has it. The price is that one store can briefly be ahead of another, which the next lesson deals with.

Each derived store is the output of code run over the log. A batch job, like the nightly Iceberg copy, reads a fixed pile once. A stream job, like the fraud features, handles each payment as it arrives. Either way, a store is only as right as the order it reads the log in, so that's next.

try.title: Take one store down for three minutes
steps: Run the demo from the labs folder. It plays ten minutes of payments, 50 a second, with the search engine down from minute 3 to minute 6. It runs them through two designs: a log with four consumers (async in the output, copying later), and one all-or-nothing write to all five stores (sync).
Predict before you run it: how many payments does each design turn away? How far behind does the search engine fall in the log design?
Look at the lines for the cache, the warehouse (finance's copy) and the fraud features. Why are they untouched in one design and part of the outage in the other?

code.title: ContainmentDemo.kt (excerpt)
code.html: // async: each consumer reads the log at its own pace for (store in stores) { val up = !(store == "search" && s in down) if (up) position[store] = minOf(logEnd, position.getValue(store) + drainPerSecond) } // sync: a payment counts only if all five systems take it if (s in down) failed += rate else accepted += rate

try.expect:
async (log + consumers): 30,000 payments accepted, 0 failed
  search     max lag  9,000 records
  cache      max lag      0 records
  warehouse  max lag      0 records
  fraud      max lag      0 records
  search caught up 5 s after it came back
sync (all-or-nothing):   21,000 payments accepted, 9,000 failed
  every store but search was healthy for the whole ten minutes

Three minutes at 50 a second is 9,000 payments. The log design turns them into 9,000 records of lag (how far a consumer is behind the end of the log) in one store, worked off at about 2,000 a second when it returns. The all-or-nothing design turns them into 9,000 failed payments, because one store that can't save stops everyone. The other three stores were fine all along, and in the log design their consumers never noticed.

aside.title: If the log has every change, why is PostgreSQL the record and not the log?
aside.html: Because PostgreSQL is where each payment is decided and saved first. The log is a faithful copy of its changes, in the order they were saved. Some companies turn this around: the program writes each event to the log first, and the database is derived from the log too. That design is event sourcing, from Event sourcing and CQRS in the Stream processing track. Either way works, as long as you can name the one place where each fact is decided.

sections.h: One log gives every copy the same order, until it can't
sections.html:
Order matters more than it looks. Payment pay-77 has two events: CAPTURED at 10:00:01, when the money moved to the shop, then REFUNDED at 10:04:30. A consumer that applies them the other way round ends with the payment captured, forever.

Copies stay identical when each one starts the same and applies the same changes in the same order, with code that gives the same output for the same input. Total order broadcast and the many faces of consensus, in the Consistency and consensus track, called this state machine replication. A log is a cheap way to get it. Every record gets one position, called its offset (0, 1, 2 and on), and every consumer reads in offset order, like lines in a notebook.

One order for everything has limits, and a growing company meets each of them.

  1. Speed. One machine, the log's leader, hands out every offset, so its speed caps the log. Past that, you split the log into several logs called partitions (Producers I: keys, partitions and ordering, in the Messaging and logs track), and order exists only inside one partition. Send a payment's events to one partition, chosen by its id, and pay-77's capture and refund stay in order. Two different payments have no order between them.
  2. Regions. With a leader in each of several regions far apart (Many leaders, in the Replication track), a write in Frankfurt and one in Virginia have no agreed order.
  3. Teams. The team that handles disputes (complaints that a charge was wrong) and the payments team each run their own program with its own log. Nothing orders a dispute decision against a refund.
  4. Offline phones. An app that saves changes on the phone first (Local-first software and sync engines) sees an order the server learns hours later.

Why not build one bigger order? Agreeing on one order across machines is the problem called consensus, and the usual ways of reaching it send every decision through one leader. So past one partition, order only what is causally related, events where one happened because of the other, and write that link into the data.

Here's a case. A customer disputes a charge. A support agent decides it for the customer in the disputes program, sees it saved, and issues the refund in the payments program a few seconds later. A third program, the shop notifier, reads both logs. For each refund it looks for a dispute. No dispute means the shop chose to refund, which costs the shop a 15.00 fee.

The disputes log reaches the notifier through a CDC program that runs up to 2.5 seconds behind. In the Try it, 76 of 1,000 refunds arrive before the decision that caused them, and 76 shops pay a fee they don't owe.

The fix is to carry the cause. The refund names the decision it came from (its id, or its offset in the disputes log), and the notifier holds a refund until it has read the disputes log that far. The wrong fees drop to zero. The 76 held refunds wait 364 ms in the middle case (the median), 1,255 ms at the longest. No library does this for you: each causal link is a field someone has to add.

Next, we'll meet a famous design that got its order right and wrote all its code twice.

try.title: Two logs, and a refund that overtakes its cause
steps: Run the demo. It decides 1,000 disputes in one log, and the agent issues each refund in the other log 1 to 6 seconds later. The disputes log reaches the notifier 0.1 to 2.5 seconds late, the payments log 50 to 300 ms late.
Predict: what share of refunds does the notifier see before their decision? A tenth of a percent, a few percent, or half?
Read the second run's rule in the excerpt. The notifier now waits, so what did the fix cost, and who pays it?

code.title: CausalityDemo.kt (excerpt)
code.html: // each consumer reads its own log in order, at its own lag val decisionSeen = seenTimes(disputes.map { it.decidedAt }, 100, 2_500) val refundSeen = ... // payments log, 50 to 300 ms val wrong = disputes.indices.count { refundSeen[it] < decisionSeen[it] } // with the link: hold a refund until its decision has been read val handled = disputes.indices.map { maxOf(refundSeen[it], decisionSeen[it]) }

try.expect:
no link between the logs:
  refunds handled before the decision that caused them: 76 of 1000
  refund fees charged by mistake: 1,140.00
refund carries the offset of its decision, notifier waits for it:
  refunds handled before their decision: 0 of 1000
  refunds held back: 76, median hold 364 ms, longest 1255 ms

About 8%: whenever the agent is quicker than the CDC program, the effect arrives before its cause. Each log is in perfect order on its own; the error is in the gap between them. The fix costs waiting time, and only for the refunds that would have been wrong.

refs.title: Kleppmann, Beresford and Svingen, Online Event Processing (CACM, 2019)

sections.h: Lambda: work every answer out twice, then add the two
sections.html:
By 2011, teams that worked numbers out from big piles of data had two kinds of tool, and neither was enough. Hadoop MapReduce, which splits a batch job across many machines (HDFS and MapReduce, in the Batch track), gave exact answers over all the data, hours late. Storm, an early stream processor (a program that handles events as they arrive), answered within seconds, but its jobs were hard to make exactly right and harder to repair after a bug.

On 13 October 2011, Nathan Marz, then at Twitter, proposed using both, in a blog post called "How to beat the CAP theorem". (CAP is a well-known result about what a system on many machines can promise when the network between them breaks.) His design later got a name: the lambda architecture.

His starting point: an answer is a function of all the data. So keep every event, unchanged, in one master dataset. A batch layer works every answer out again from all of it every few hours, on Hadoop, and stores the results, called batch views. A speed layer handles only the events since the last batch run, with Storm writing realtime views to a fast database. To answer a question, the app reads both and adds them.

Picture two clerks keeping one total for the café. One adds up the whole notebook each night. The other keeps a running tally on a slip during the day. The total is the night clerk's number plus the slip. The night clerk is the batch layer, and the slip is the speed layer.

Two of Marz's ideas outlived his design. The input never changes, so a bug can't destroy data, and the fix for a bad answer is to work it out again. And mistakes in the speed layer are temporary, because the next batch run replaces them.

The cost is that every piece of logic exists twice, in two systems. Take one of the fraud features, a card's spend over the last 24 hours. The batch version is a query in Spark, a program that runs batch jobs on many machines. The speed version is a job in Flink, a program that runs stream jobs. One subtracts refunds and the other forgets to. One converts currencies with yesterday's rates, the other with today's. Every morning, when a batch run replaces the speed layer's numbers, the feature jumps for thousands of cards, a step no customer caused. Our two clerks count refunds differently.

Jay Kreps, who helped create Kafka at LinkedIn, made the case against lambda in July 2014. Keeping code in two different systems perfectly in step was very hard, he found, and better tools wouldn't fix it. Every bug fix, format change and release happens twice, on two sets of machines. Designing Data-Intensive Applications (2nd edition), the book much of this track follows, reports that lambda has fallen out of use.

Two copies of the logic drift apart. Keep one. Kreps also proposed how, and that's next.

try.title: Find where the two layers disagree
steps: Below are the two layers of one lambda feature, "spend per card over the last 24 hours". Read both and list every way they can give different answers for the same card at the same moment. There are at least four.

The first is SQL, the language databases understand. It takes the payments of the last 24 hours, converts each amount to euros with a table of exchange rates, and adds them up per card. The second is a Kotlin function the stream job calls for each new payment.

-- batch layer, Spark SQL, runs at 02:00 and 14:00 UTC
SELECT card_id, sum(amount_eur) AS spend_24h
FROM lake.payments p
JOIN lake.fx_rates r ON r.currency = p.currency AND r.day = current_date - 1
WHERE p.status IN ('CAPTURED', 'REFUNDED')
  AND p.event_time >= current_timestamp - INTERVAL 24 HOURS
GROUP BY card_id

// speed layer, a stream job: adds each payment as it arrives
fun onPayment(p: Payment) {
    if (p.status != "CAPTURED") return
    val eur = p.amount * liveRates.getValue(p.currency)
    spend.merge(p.cardId, eur, Double::plus)      // expired by a 24 h timer per entry
}
Then decide: which of these differences would kappa, the next section's design with one job for both history and live data, remove?
try.expect:
1. Refunds: the batch layer adds captures and refunds together (and if refunds are stored as positive amounts, it adds them to the spend); the speed layer skips refunds. 2. Exchange rates: yesterday's rate table against live rates. 3. Time: the batch layer filters on event_time, when the payment happened. The speed layer counts what arrived in the last 24 hours by its own timer, which is processing time, when the job saw it. So a late upload counts in one and not the other. 4. Arithmetic: the speed layer adds doubles (numbers with binary fractions), the batch layer probably exact decimals, so totals differ in the last cent. 5. The seam: at 02:00 and 14:00 the batch result replaces up to 12 hours of speed-layer numbers at once.

Kappa removes 1, 2, 4 and 5, because there is one piece of code and nothing to add together. It doesn't remove 3 on its own: one job that uses processing time is wrong the same way every time. The next section shows how badly.

refs.title: Nathan Marz, How to beat the CAP theorem (2011)
Jay Kreps, Questioning the Lambda Architecture (O'Reilly Radar, 2014)

sections.h: Kappa: keep the log, replay it into a second copy, switch the readers
sections.html:
Kreps's alternative fits in four steps, and he suggested, half joking, calling it the kappa architecture.

  1. Keep the input in a log for as long as you might need to work it out again. To rebuild 30 days, keep 30 days. Kafka deletes records older than 7 days by default, through the setting retention.ms (Partitions and segments on disk, in the Messaging and logs track). So you change it on purpose, or keep older records somewhere cheaper, such as an Iceberg copy.
  2. When the logic changes, start a second copy of the job with the new code. It reads from the beginning of the log and writes to a new table.
  3. When it has caught up with the end of the log, switch the app to the new table.
  4. Stop the old job and delete the old table.

There is one engine and one codebase. History is the oldest part of the log, so replaying it is the batch job. At the café, it's one clerk with one method, who starts a fresh sheet from the notebook's first page whenever the method changes. Here the picture breaks in our favour: a program rereads a month in minutes, and can do it again tomorrow.

Designing Data-Intensive Applications names three conditions for one engine to do both jobs. The engine must replay old events through the same code that handles new ones, which a kept log gives you. A crash during the replay must not count anything twice, which is called exactly-once processing (Fault tolerance in stream processing). And any grouping by time must use event time, the time written in the record when the payment happened. Processing time, the time on the job's clock when it handles the record, won't do (Time in streams, in the Stream processing track).

The third condition is the one that bites. Two copies of the new job, v2, replay 30 days of payments. One puts each payment on the day it handled it, the other on the day the payment happened. The first puts 554,322.25 on today and zero on every earlier day, the warm-up's answer. The live job had used processing time for a year and looked right, because live, a payment is handled within a second of happening. Only the few late uploads landed on the wrong day, and nobody noticed. A replay handles every record now, so the hidden mistake becomes the whole answer.

Apache Beam (2.77.0, October 2026), a library built on Google's Dataflow model, lets you write one pipeline for both. It runs on Flink, Spark or Google Cloud Dataflow, over a fixed pile or a stream. Flink and Spark can also handle both kinds of input on their own.

Replays take real time, so size them first. In the Try it, v2 reads 400 records a minute while 5 new ones arrive, so it gains 395 a minute. On 6,000 records of history, that's 6,000 / 395, rounded up: 16 minutes. A busy log that gets 50,000 records a second holds 130 billion after a month.

Next, we'll move the readers across without anyone seeing a gap.

try.title: Replay a month, by processing time and by event time
steps: Run the demo. It builds the lab's 30 days of history, then replays them into two copies of v2 at 400 records a minute: one groups payments by processing time, one by event time.
Before you look: on which day will the processing-time copy put the month's takings?
Run it again with -Pargs=100 (100 records a minute). Which numbers change, and which stay exactly the same?

code.title: ReplayDemo.kt (excerpt)
code.html: for (i in position until stop) { // processing time: the minute the job handles the record (today, for all of them) v2Processing.merge(log[i].merchant to now / DAY, net(log[i]), Long::plus) // event time: the minute the payment happened, carried inside the record v2Event.merge(log[i].merchant to log[i].eventTime / DAY, net(log[i]), Long::plus) }

try.expect:
v2 read 6,080 records in 16 minutes (400 a minute, 5 new a minute)

net revenue, all merchants, by day:
  day   v2 by processing time   v2 by event time
    0                    0.00          19,684.20
    1                    0.00          19,139.78
    2                    0.00          19,609.06
  ...
   28                    0.00          17,678.19
   29                    0.00          19,785.49
   30              554,322.25           6,846.18

Net revenue is takings minus refunds, in this demo for all shops together. The processing-time copy puts the whole month on day 30, the day of the replay. The event-time copy matches what a batch job over the same records works out. With -Pargs=100 the replay takes 64 minutes and reads 6,320 records (the extra minutes bring more live payments), and the event-time numbers for days 0 to 29 don't change by a cent. The answer depends on the log, not on how fast you replayed it.

refs.title: Akidau et al., The Dataflow Model (PVLDB 8(12), 2015)

video.title: Reprocessing: replay into v2 while v1 serves, then switch

sections.h: Changing a table's shape, with a way back at every step
sections.html:
Back to finance's change from the opening. The old table, v1 (daily_gross), stores gross takings per shop per day, before refunds, by processing time. The new one, v2 (daily_net), needs refunds, which v1 threw away, and event-time days, which v1 got wrong for every late upload. Schemas that evolve, in the Encoding track, gave rules for changing a data format safely, such as adding an optional field. Those rules cover changes that add something, and this one doesn't. The facts v2 needs aren't in v1 at all. They're in the log, so v2 is worked out from the log again, next to v1.

The stepper walks through it. v2 replays from offset 0 while v1 keeps serving. While v2 is behind, nobody moves to it, because a half-built table is missing the recent days. When v2's lag reaches zero, we move a stable share of shops at a time. Each shop gets a bucket from 0 to 99, worked out from its id by a hash (a function that turns text into a number that looks random but never changes). Shops in buckets below 5 move first, then below 25, then everyone. A shop always stays on its side, so its dashboard doesn't flip between versions on every refresh.

For the shops on v2, compare the two tables. They should differ by the refunds and the late uploads, and by nothing else. Any other difference is a bug in v2.

Each step can be undone, because v1 never stopped. Going back, a rollback, is one change that points every reader at v1 again, and v1's table is as current as v2's. Only the last step is one-way: stop v1 and drop its table, once everyone has been on v2 long enough to trust it. After that, going back means another replay.

A table rebuilt in place has no way back. Build the new one beside it.

Plan for the recipe's costs. While both versions run, you pay for two jobs and two tables. The log must still hold everything the new version needs, so how long to keep it is decided long before the change. And a replayed job must not repeat its side effects, the things it does to the outside world. If v1 also emailed owners when their takings passed a target, v2's replay would send a month of emails again. Keep side effects out of jobs that work data out, or give each one an id so a repeat is recognised. The end-to-end argument, lesson 3 of this track, carries such an id from a phone all the way to the database.

The same recipe already runs inside a database. To build a new index on a busy table, PostgreSQL reads the table as it was, then catches up with the writes made meanwhile. From then on, it keeps the index current. The next lesson, Unbundling the database, starts there.

try.title: Argue for the gradual cutover
steps: A colleague proposes a shortcut: stop v1, move its saved position back to offset 0, put the v2 code into the same job and the same daily_gross table, and let it rebuild in place. "Same result, half the work."
Write down three things that go wrong for the owners, or for you, with the shortcut, and which step of the recipe prevents each.
try.expect:
1. For the 16 minutes of the rebuild, every shop reads a half-built table: recent days show zero or partial totals. The recipe keeps readers on v1 until v2's lag is 0.
  2. If v2 has a bug, there's no correct table to go back to, because v1's table was overwritten. The recipe keeps v1 running and current, so rollback is one switch.
  3. Every owner sees the new numbers at the same moment, so a bug reaches all of them at once, and support can't tell a v2 bug from a real change. The stable 5%, 25%, 100% shift limits who sees a bug, and lets you compare v1 and v2 for the same shop. Also good answers: the rebuilt table mixes old rows written by v1 with new rows written by v2 if it isn't emptied first; and any side effects in the job run again during the rebuild.

refs.title: Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, chapter 13 (reprocessing for evolution)

opening:
Picture the café where this course began. You tap your card for a coffee, and the payments app writes one line about it: which card, which shop, how much and when. Within a second, it also shows up in the owner's takings (the money her shop took today), in support's search and in a fraud check.

Now finance asks for one change: takings should subtract refunds, and count each payment on the day it happened. A month of numbers must be worked out again, while two thousand owners keep looking at theirs.

The tempting plan is to change the code, empty the table and let it refill. One program and one table feel like less work. Until it refills, every owner sees a month with holes.

Choosing an engine ended with one log feeding a company's tools. In this lesson, we'll trace every copy to one record, see where one order of events stops, and meet two designs, lambda and kappa. Then we'll redo the month without a gap. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with finance asking for a month of takings worked out again, while two thousand owners kept reading theirs. We replayed the log into a second table by event time, moved the owners across a few at a time, and kept the old table until nobody needed the way back.

Find a card statement, on paper or in your bank's app. Many show two dates for each payment: the day you paid, and the day the bank posted it. That's event time and processing time, side by side. Look for a weekend payment where they differ.

Next, we'll look inside one database, find the same machinery already there, and ask what happens when we take it out.

worked.title: Move the dashboard from v1 to v2 with Kreps's recipe

steps.say: Size the replay. The new job must read the whole history while new records keep arriving. If it reads R records a minute, L new ones arrive each minute and H are already in the log, it catches up after H / (R - L) minutes. If R isn't much bigger than L, it never catches up.
steps.code:
H = 6,000 records of history
R = 400 records a minute (the v2 job)
L = 5 records a minute (live traffic)

minutes = ceil(6,000 / (400 - 5)) = ceil(15.19) = 16

steps.say: Start v2 from offset 0, into its own table. A new job starts at the beginning of the log. In Kafka, that's a new consumer group with auto.offset.reset=earliest, writing to an output table with a new name.
steps.code: fun startV2(view: View, batch: Int): Job { check(v2 == null) { "v2 is already running" } require(view !== v1.view) { "v2 needs its own table" } return Job("v2", log, view, batch).also { v2 = it } // position 0 }

steps.say: Refuse to move readers while v2 is behind. A table that has replayed half the log is missing the recent half of the days.
steps.code: fun shift(percent: Int): Boolean { val job = v2 ?: return false if (job.lag > 0) return false // still replaying percentOnV2 = percent // one assignment: atomic return true }

steps.say: Move a stable share, and read each shop from one table. The bucket comes from the shop's id, so the same shop always gets the same version.
steps.code: fun read(merchant: String, day: Long): Answer { val job = if (bucketOf(merchant) < percentOnV2) v2!! else v1 return Answer(job.name, job.view.cents(merchant, day)) }

steps.say: Keep the way back until the end. Rollback works while v1 runs. Retiring v1 is allowed only at 100%, and after that, rollback is refused.
steps.code: fun rollback() { check(!v1Retired) { "v1 is retired; there is nothing to roll back to" } percentOnV2 = 0 } fun retireV1() { check(percentOnV2 == 100) { "move every reader to v2 first" } v1.stop() // drops daily_gross v1Retired = true }

lab.title: Replay a month into v2 and cut over without losing a reader
steps: Run the tests once from the labs folder. All 10 fail.

Read Log.kt and World.kt; both are finished. EventLog is the kept log. Job is a stream job with its own position and a lag, how far it is behind the end of the log. World plays 30 days of history through v1, then moves one minute forward per tick, with 5 new payments a minute. Its first live payment is a late upload from yesterday at 23:50.
In Migration.kt, write startV2, shift, rollback, retireV1 and read. Each is two to four lines, and the comment above each one says when to refuse. Then the six tests in MigrationTest pass.

Now look at ReprocessingTest: its three tests still fail. DailyNet in Views.kt copied v1's habit of putting each record on the day it was handled (processedAt). Read the failure for replay does not pile thirty days of revenue into today, then fix the one line so each record counts on the day it happened.

Run the tests again until all 10 pass. ReplayPropertyTest uses jqwik, a library that runs one test on many random inputs. It replays 30 random worlds in random chunk sizes, and checks that v2 always equals the answer a batch job gives, however the replay was chunked.
hints: startV2: Job("v2", log, view, batch) already starts at position 0. Check check(v2 == null) first, and store the job in v2 before returning it.
shift: val job = v2 ?: return false, then return false while job.lag > 0. Set percentOnV2 only when you return true.
read: if (bucketOf(merchant) < percentOnV2) v2!! else v1 picks the job, and Answer(job.name, job.view.cents(merchant, day)) is the answer.
DailyNet.apply: the record carries e.eventTime. dayOf(e.eventTime) is the day the payment happened; processedAt is the day this job ran.

drill.title: Kreps's recipe from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write the four steps of Kreps's recipe, the three things one engine needs to handle both history and live data, and when shift agrees to move readers.

answer.html:
Recipe
1. Retain the input log as long as you may need to reprocess (30 days -> retain 30 days).
2. Start a second job with the new code, from offset 0, writing a NEW table.
3. When it has caught up, switch readers to the new table.
4. Stop the old job and delete the old table (keep both briefly for rollback).

One engine for batch and stream needs
- replayable input (the retained log, or files on object storage)
- exactly-once state: a crash mid-replay doesn't double-count
- event-time windows: during a replay, processing time is "now" for every record

shift(percent) accepts only when v2 exists and v2.lag == 0;
rollback only while v1 still runs; retire v1 only at 100%.

recap: A company keeps one system of record for each fact and many derived stores worked out from it. Feed them all from one log of changes (change data capture), so each store can only be behind, never on a path of its own.

A log gives every reader the same order, which keeps copies identical. One order for everything stops at one machine's speed, at regions, at separate teams' programs and at offline phones. Past that, keep order per key (one payment, one partition) and write causal links into the data.

Lambda worked every answer out twice, in a batch layer and a speed layer, and added the two when asked. Its lasting ideas are input that never changes and answers worked out again; its flaw is two codebases that drift apart.
Kappa keeps the input in a log, replays it from offset 0 into a new table with a second copy of the job, moves readers when that copy has caught up, and only then retires the old one.
One engine handles history and live data only with a replayable log, exactly-once processing and grouping by event time. Grouping by processing time puts a whole replay on today.

The limit: a replay costs time, two jobs and two tables while both run, and a log kept long enough, decided months before you need it. Side effects such as emails must stay out of the replayed job, or carry an id that marks a repeat.

explain.prompt: A teammate asks why changing the fraud features will take a week with two versions running, instead of one release on Tuesday. Explain the plan, and what each part protects against.
explain.answer: The features are worked out from the payments log, so the new version is built from that log, not from the old table. On Tuesday we start a second job with the new code. It reads the log from the first record and writes a new table, while the old job keeps serving. It needs a few hours to read 90 days, which is why we made the log keep 90 days last month. Nobody moves until its lag is zero, because a half-replayed table is missing the most recent days. Then we move a stable share of cards to the new table, 5%, then 25%, then everyone, and compare old and new features for the same cards. The only differences should be the ones we meant to make. Going back is one switch to the old table, which stays current because the old job never stops. After a week at 100% with clean comparisons, we stop the old job and drop its table. The new job groups by event time, so the replay gives the same answer the live path will. And it only writes features: anything that sends alerts reads them from outside the job, so the replay doesn't send a month of alerts again.

deeper.html:
Where kappa's ideas came from. In December 2013, Kreps wrote an essay on LinkedIn's engineering blog, "The Log: What every software engineer should know about real-time data's unifying abstraction". It argued that a company's whole flow of data looks like one big database, with the log as its record of changes and every derived system as one of its indexes. Kappa is that essay applied to changing code.

One codebase for two engines. Twitter's Summingbird let a team write a feature once and turned it into a batch job and a stream job. Kreps granted that it helped, but you still ran two systems, and you could use only the features both of them had. He also rejected the claim in Marz's title: lambda doesn't get around the CAP theorem.

Lambda's original post is worth reading for what it got right. Marz's "How to beat the CAP theorem" is mostly an argument for data that never changes and for working answers out again. Complexity comes from data that changes in place and from updating answers bit by bit, so he kept those in one layer whose mistakes are temporary. The batch layer was, in effect, a scheduled replay. Kappa kept that idea and dropped the second codebase.

The Dataflow model's four questions. The Dataflow model (Akidau and colleagues at Google, 2015) treats a fixed pile of data as a special case of a stream that never ends. Beam describes every pipeline by four questions, and Flink uses the same ideas under other names: what is computed, where in event time it belongs, when in processing time a result is sent out, and how a later result corrects an earlier one. "When" is answered by watermarks and triggers. A watermark is the engine's estimate that no more events before some time T will arrive, and a trigger says when to send a result, perhaps early and then corrected. Time in streams, in the Stream processing track, builds these.

Replays at scale. A month of a busy log can be billions of records. So teams often start the new job from a snapshot, a copy of the data as it was at one moment (a lakehouse table, or the old job's saved state), and continue from the log at the offset where the snapshot was taken. That's the same copy-then-catch-up pattern the next lesson finds inside PostgreSQL's CREATE INDEX.

The framing of data integration, the limits of one order and the joining of batch and stream follow Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, chapter 13, which says plainly that it argues for one view of streaming systems.
